summary: Analyzes what a routing protocol needs to do in industrial plants that use low-power, lossy wireless networks of field devices such as sensors and actuators. It lists functional requirements around reliability, latency, and security. It is an informational requirements document, not a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine a factory full of tiny wireless sensors that sometimes lose their messages. This document lists what a postal system for them must be able to do so important notes still arrive safely and on time.

subtitle: What a routing protocol must do for battery-powered wireless sensors and actuators in industrial plants.

tldr.problem: Wireless, low-power field devices are being added to industrial plants, but there is no open standard for routing over such Low-power and Lossy Networks (LLNs), so even ISA100.11a leaves routing to proprietary methods.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes industrial traffic, topologies and constraints and turns them into functional requirements for an IPv6 routing protocol: multiple paths, constraint-based routes, node-aware routing, fast convergence, mobility support, easy provisioning and security.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document, not a protocol. It states what a ROLL routing protocol for industrial use has to achieve.

facts.label: Convergence after a device is added
facts.value: MUST within several minutes, SHOULD within tens of seconds

today: RFC 5673 is an Informational requirements document, published in October 2009, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines no protocol and sets no standard.

sections.title: Why Industrial Routing Needs Its Own Requirements
sections.content:
Information Technology is increasingly applied to industrial Control Technology, and many vendors are extending or replacing local fieldbus technology with Ethernet and IP-based solutions. At the same time, wireless, low-power field devices are being introduced. IPv6 sits where both trends meet. The ISA100.11a specification, for example, adapts the IEEE 802.15.4 PHY and MAC, 6LoWPAN and UDP to industrial use.

The gap is routing. Because there are no open standards for routing in Low-power and Lossy Networks (LLNs), even ISA100.11a leaves routing to proprietary methods. This document analyzes the requirements of the industrial environment for an IPv6-based LLN routing protocol. It uses RFC 2119 words, so MUST, SHOULD and MAY mark how strict each requirement is.
sections.plainLanguage: Factories are adding little wireless gadgets, but each maker has its own secret way to pass messages along. This document says what an open, shared way should be able to do.

sections.title: Applications and Traffic Patterns
sections.content:
The RFC expects wireless to augment wire, not replace it, because cable is seen as more proven and safer. For LLNs to be adopted, the wireless network needs three qualities: low power, high reliability, and easy installation and maintenance. Industrial automation splits into process control (a fluid product such as oil or gas) and discrete manufacturing (individual items), and process control tolerates more latency.

Process applications fall into six classes under three categories: safety (class 0), control (classes 1 to 3) and monitoring (classes 4 and 5). Timely delivery matters more as the class number falls, and for control, jitter is as important as latency. Industrial users are interested in wireless for monitoring classes 4 and 5 and for the non-critical parts of classes 2 and 3.

Most near-term LLN traffic is low-frequency data collection: 90% of the market is covered by packet rates between 1/second and 1/hour, with an average under 1/minute. Some sensors, such as vibration monitors, are bursty. Time-critical alarm packets are expected to get lower latency than periodic data. Non-critical closed-loop control can need latency as low as 100 milliseconds, though many loops tolerate more than 1 second, and most users avoid wireless inside fast control loops.
sections.plainLanguage: Most factory sensors just report a number now and then, like a thermometer sending the temperature. A few messages, like alarms, are urgent and must jump the line.

sections.title: Network Topology
sections.content:
Topology is hard to generalize, but most existing applications can be met by networks of 10 to 200 field devices with a maximum of 20 hops. Field devices are assumed to do the routing themselves, in two logical roles: field routers and non-routing devices. Roles may change over time to share the cost of forwarding.

To scale, a backbone can act as a canopy over several smaller LLNs, joined to them through backbone routers. The RFC describes a refinery of several square kilometers with a self-forming, self-healing mesh that might be 5 to 10 hops across, and the opposite case where a backbone reaches nearly every node. Traffic is mostly publish/subscribe sensor data heading toward one or more sinks.

Sinks may sit on the plant network, the business (office) network or the Internet. These domains must stay logically segregated even though devices share the same radio medium. The RFC therefore says LLNs are best treated as yet another segregated domain, which means moving from perimeter security toward stronger device identity authentication. It also notes that logical topologies need not match the physical radio network, for example a control topology isolated from a monitoring topology.
sections.plainLanguage: The sensors pass messages from neighbor to neighbor, like kids passing notes along a row, until the note reaches the teacher's desk. Different kinds of notes must go to different desks.

sections.title: Routing Requirements
sections.content:
The ISA100 model groups traffic into four service categories: periodic data, event data (alarms and bursts), client/server and bulk transfer. Service parameters that can affect routing include bandwidth, latency, transmission phase, service contract type and transmission priority. Because different flows want different treatment, the routing protocol MUST support different metric types per link and MUST be able to generate different routes with different characteristics for flows between the same two endpoints. The infrastructure is REQUIRED to compute and update constrained routes on demand, and it MUST be able to compute unidirectional routes with potentially different costs over one or more non-congruent paths.

For reliability, availability is usually defined as end-to-end delivery within a bounded latency, and the RFC argues that a single figure like 99.9% creates more confusion than clarity. It notes that HART7 sets user availability expectations at 99.9%. Because link stability is low, path diversity is critical, and the protocol MUST compute paths of not-necessarily-equal cost to enable load-balancing. Undetected corrupted data is often more dangerous than missing data.

Devices vary: battery-powered with lifetimes of at least five years are most common, and energy-scavenging devices have both long-term and short-term power limits. The routing algorithm MUST support node-constrained routing that accounts for power and memory.

  • Multicast: the protocol SHOULD support it.
  • Convergence: after a new device is added, it MUST converge within several minutes and SHOULD converge within tens of seconds.
  • Mobility: SHOULD support walking speeds for handheld devices and vehicular speeds of up to 35 kmph.
sections.plainLanguage: The postal system must send alarms by the fastest road and reports by cheaper roads. It must have backup routes, notice when a sensor's battery is low, and work out new routes quickly when something new joins.

sections.title: Manageability and Conflicting Goals
sections.content:
The process industry is manpower constrained, so installing a wireless sensor should require no new skills. Most users want plug-and-play provisioning with strong, automated authentication so networks can accept or reject new joiners. The routing protocol SHOULD be fully configurable over the air as part of joining. It SHOULD NOT require preprovisioned information about the deployment environment, and it MUST enable full discovery of links, peers and reachable network. It MUST also allow its own configuration to be distributed by an external mechanism from a centralized management controller.

The RFC admits that some requirements look antagonistic. Power economy conflicts with the need to spend more energy on a short emergency path, easy provisioning conflicts with strong security, and convergence time conflicts with network size. The stated convergence times apply to an average network with tens of devices, and a backbone can allow growth to thousands of nodes. Growing convergence time reasonably with network size is acceptable.
sections.plainLanguage: Setting up a sensor should be as easy as plugging in a lamp, but it also has to be safe from strangers. Sometimes two good goals pull against each other, and the document says so openly.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Industrial wireless networks have substantial financial and human safety implications, so security is of considerable concern. The RFC separates temporary loss of connectivity, such as from a thunderstorm, from attacks by knowledgeable adversaries. It points out that an LLN access point can act as a wireless backdoor onto legacy wired plant networks, so the access point itself must guarantee domain segregation.

Field devices must be assumed to have marginal physical security and might be compromised. The routing protocol SHOULD limit the risk from one compromised node, for example by using non-congruent paths and balancing traffic. It SHOULD compartmentalize trust, and it MUST be configured and managed using secure messages and protocols. Because nodes can route, end-node security requirements are usually a superset of router requirements. Implications for the routing protocol itself are left as future work.
sections.plainLanguage: Sensors sit out in the open where someone could tamper with one. The system should make sure one tricked sensor cannot ruin the rest, and the door between the wireless network and the factory computers must stay locked.
